content: 1. The GRADE Working Group classifies evidence into four levels of certainty: high, moderate, low, and very low. High certainty indicates that the true effect is very likely to be close to the estimated effect. Moderate certainty suggests that the true effect is probably close to the estimate, but there is a possibility of substantial differences. Low certainty reflects limited confidence in the estimate, with the true effect potentially differing significantly. Very low certainty indicates minimal confidence, with the true effect likely to be substantially different from the estimate. 2. Evidence can be downgraded for various reasons: One level for serious risk of bias due to limitations in study design and execution. Two levels for very serious imprecision, such as few events and wide confidence intervals that include no effect, potential benefit, and potential harm. One level for serious inconsistency, such as high heterogeneity (e.g., I² = 75% or 66%). One level for serious imprecision when studies are underpowered to detect differences between groups. One level for risk of bias due to study design limitations. 3. Secondary prophylaxis for visceral leishmaniasis (VL) in HIV co-infected patients was evaluated in several studies. A retrospective cohort study from India (2017) assessed the efficacy of secondary prophylaxis with liposomal amphotericin B or amphotericin B deoxycholate compared to no prophylaxis in 53 patients. The evidence was deemed very uncertain due to serious limitations in study design and imprecision. 4. Two non-comparative prospective cohort studies from Ethiopia (2015 and 2019) evaluated pentamidine as secondary prophylaxis following initial VL cure. The evidence on the effect of pentamidine compared to no prophylaxis was also very uncertain. 5. Regarding all-cause mortality: In the Indian study (2017), no participants (0/27) died in the amphotericin B group, while 11/24 died in the no-prophylaxis group at one-year follow-up. In the Ethiopian study (2019), 5/29 patients died within one year of pentamidine prophylaxis. Another Ethiopian study (2015) reported 5/71 deaths within two years of follow-up. 6. Relapse rates were reported in all three studies: In the Ethiopian study (2019), 12 participants (41%) relapsed within one year of pentamidine prophylaxis. In the Ethiopian study (2015), 20 participants (27%) relapsed within two years. 7. Relapse-free survival was also assessed: The Ethiopian study (2015) reported a six-month relapse-free survival probability of 79% (95% CI: 67–87%), 71% at one year (95% CI: 59–80%), and 53% at 24–36 months. The Ethiopian study (2019) reported a one-year relapse-free survival rate of 46% (95% CI: 26–63%) for patients receiving pentamidine. 8. Serious adverse events (SAEs) were reported in two single-arm studies assessing pentamidine: The Ethiopian study (2015) reported 21 SAEs in 17/74 patients (23%) at one-year follow-up, with two events (renal failure in patients hospitalized with pneumonia) possibly related to pentamidine. The Ethiopian study (2019) reported 8/29 patients (28%) experiencing SAEs at one year, including one death due to acute renal failure in a patient with multiple coexisting conditions. 9. Adverse events related to pentamidine were reported in one study (Ethiopia 2015). At one-year follow-up, 42 drug-related adverse events occurred in 30/74 participants (41%). These included the need for additional intravenous fluids during pentamidine administration, reduced infusion rates, oral hydration, prolonged hospital observation, additional medications, and glucose supplementation. 10. Treatment adherence was reported in two studies: In the Ethiopian study (2015), 41/74 participants (55%) completed follow-up, taking at least 11/12 doses without experiencing relapse, death, or drug-related SAEs. In the Ethiopian study (2019), 22/29 participants (76%) achieved full compliance with monthly pentamidine infusions. 11. Patient satisfaction with secondary prophylaxis was not reported in any of the included studies. 12. The study populations consisted of adults aged 18 years and older, with mean ages ranging from 32 to 37 years across studies. No studies reported intervention effects stratified by age or gender. 13. Health status was reported in one study (Ethiopia 2015), where 76% of participants were malnourished. Other demographic or social factors, such as place of residence, race, socioeconomic status, or personal characteristics, were not reported. 14. Acceptability of treatments was influenced by the teratogenic potential of miltefosine, requiring assured contraception during treatment and for four months afterward. Oral contraceptives were deemed inadequate due to the high prevalence of vomiting and diarrhea associated with miltefosine treatment. 15. The evidence for secondary prophylaxis in VL-HIV co-infected patients remains very uncertain due to serious limitations in study design, imprecision, and reliance on non-comparative studies. Further high-quality research is needed to establish the efficacy and safety of these interventions.
